name: The Great Oxidation Event
statement: Around 2.4 billion years ago, oxygen from photosynthesis first built up in the air, transforming the planet.
statementAccent: oxygen from photosynthesis first built up
meaning: The Great Oxidation Event was the interval in the early Paleoproterozoic, roughly 2.4 to 2.0 billion years ago, when free molecular oxygen, produced by oxygenic photosynthesis in cyanobacteria, first accumulated to geochemically significant levels in Earth's atmosphere and shallow oceans. To the anaerobic life then dominant, oxygen was toxic, so the event is dramatically called the oxygen catastrophe. It was one of the most profound transformations in Earth's history, reshaping the atmosphere, the chemistry of the oceans, and the trajectory of life, though it did not yet bring oxygen anywhere near modern levels.
mechanism: Oxygenic photosynthesis had likely evolved somewhat earlier, but oxygen did not accumulate at first because it was consumed by reducing sinks: dissolved ferrous iron in the oceans, which oxidised and precipitated as banded iron formations, and reduced volcanic gases. Only once the flux of oxygen, tied to the burial of organic carbon and other reductants, exceeded the capacity of these sinks did oxygen spill over into the atmosphere. The rise then destroyed atmospheric methane, a strong greenhouse gas, oxidising it to weaker carbon dioxide, which helped trigger the severe Huronian glaciation, and it began building a protective ozone layer.

examples.text: Mass-independent fractionation of sulfur isotopes, produced under an oxygen-poor sky, disappears from rocks after about 2.4 billion years ago, the single most important marker that atmospheric oxygen rose above a threshold.
Extensive banded iron formations record an ocean shedding dissolved iron, while continental redbeds coloured by oxidised iron mark the onset of oxidative weathering on land.
Rising oxygen oxidised the methane that had warmed the Archean atmosphere, helping to trigger the Huronian glaciation, a possible Snowball Earth.

variants.name: The later Neoproterozoic rise
variants.text: A second major oxygenation, roughly 850 to 540 million years ago, that pushed oxygen toward higher though still sub-modern levels; the Great Oxidation Event did not produce modern oxygen.

variants.name: Whiffs of early oxygen
variants.text: Evidence for transient, localised oxygen around 2.5 billion years ago, before the permanent rise, indicating oxygen production preceded its accumulation, though such whiffs are debated.

whyItMatters: It is one of the most significant transformations in Earth's history, moving the planet from an essentially anoxic world to one with free oxygen, an ozone shield, and the eventual biochemical basis for aerobic, energy-rich metabolism and complex life. It reshaped ocean chemistry, ended and later renewed banded iron deposition, and is linked to the first great glaciations. It stands as the clearest early example of life fundamentally and irreversibly altering the whole planet's surface environment.

working.text: read the event as when oxygen built up, not when photosynthesis began, since oxygen sinks delayed its rise.
use the disappearance of mass-independent sulfur fractionation as the key sign that atmospheric oxygen crossed a threshold.
remember oxygen rose only to a small fraction of the present level, with the climb to modern values coming far later.

limits: The event is well-established across independent geochemical proxies, but its precise timing, tempo, and consequences remain debated. Modern scholarship increasingly frames it as a protracted process over tens to hundreds of millions of years rather than an instantaneous flip, and transient earlier whiffs of oxygen are reported and disputed. The claim that it was the largest mass extinction by proportion is an inference, not a direct observation, since the microbial record is far too sparse to document such a die-off, and it is typically not counted among the conventional great extinctions. Billion-year dates are proxy-dependent and approximate.
misreadings: Oxygen did not reach modern levels of about twenty-one percent during the event; post-event levels were on the order of a few percent or less, with the rise to near-modern values coming much later. It was not necessarily a single abrupt catastrophe, its tempo being debated. Cyanobacteria and oxygenic photosynthesis likely predate the accumulation, so the event marks when oxygen built up, not when it was first produced. And the mass extinction of anaerobes, while a plausible and popular framing, is an inference rather than an established fact.
origin: A well-evidenced episode of the early Paleoproterozoic, its concept formalised by researchers including Preston Cloud and Heinrich Holland, with the key sulfur-isotope proxy established by James Farquhar and colleagues in 2000.

sources.text: Great Oxidation Event, Wikipedia. — the ~2.4 Ga rise, the oxygen-sink mechanism, the sulfur marker, and the consequences.
Farquhar, Bao, and Thiemens, 'Atmospheric Influence of Earth's Earliest Sulfur Cycle,' Science 289 (2000): 756-758. — the mass-independent sulfur-isotope evidence for the oxygenation threshold.
